newsitem.title: INDIA: India ministry says no plan now to raise oil price.
newsitem.headline: India ministry says no plan now to raise oil price.

text.p: The Indian Petroleum Ministry said on Wednesday that there was no plan for an immediate increase in petroleum prices.
"There is nothing afoot on increase in petroleum prices. It is not immediate," a ministry official who asked not to be named told Reuters.
Share prices on the Bombay Stock Exchange were hit on Wednesday by reports that an increase in petroleum prices appeared certain.
The Indian Express newspaper said the Petroleum Ministry had sought the cabinet's approval to raise the price of crude oil paid to state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd.
The paper said the ministry had sought a rise in the price of crude oil extracted by the oil-producing companies to 1,991 rupees per tonne from 1,741 rupees.
It said the ministry had also recommended that the hike should be passed on to consumers through increases in the prices of petroleum products.
"I can neither confirm nor deny the report," the Petroleum Ministry official said.
Under India's administered pricing mechanism, refining companies are paid on a cost-plus basis with reimbursement of input costs and a 15 percent return on the net worth.
The ministry official said discussions were underway within the ministry on how to meet the oil pool deficit.
Under the oil pool account, the government reimburses oil firms for the difference between what they pay to import crude and what domestic refiners pay them.
Ministry officials estimate that the oil pool deficit is expected to touch 155 billion rupees in 1996/97 (April-March) against 57 billion rupees last year.
Junior Petroleum Minister T. R. Baalu said earlier this month that a revision of domestic prices of oil products would depend on the collective decision of the federal cabinet.
"As things stand I am not interested in increasing the prices," Baalu said at the time.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government raised petroleum prices shortly after taking office in June, sparking a bitter row within the 13-party coalition.
India's crude oil and petroleum product prices are administered by the government. Farmers and low-income groups are supplied diesel and kerosene at subsidised rates.

An ONGC official said on Wednesday that a increase in the price of crude paid to oil companies was overdue. "This revision has been pending for 18 months," he told Reuters. But the official said ONGC had not yet received any concrete proposal from the government.

India spent about $6.5 billion in 1995/96 (April-March) to import some 22 million to 23 million tonnes of crude and 16 million tonnes of refined products. That accounted for some 20 percent of the total value of imports.
Oil output in 1996/97 is expected to dip to 32 million tonnes against an earlier estimate of 33.7 million tonnes.
Finance Ministry officials said the oil import bill for 1996/97 was now estimated at $9.0 billion, against a previously calculated $7.8 billion, due to higher world crude prices.
